articles.title: In 1928, Al Capone bought a Miami Beach estate and spent about $200,000 fortifying it; after the mansion was demolished in 2023, its vacant site sold for $21 million
articles.summary: Real Estate News: In 1928, at the height of his reign as Chicago’s most notorious gangster, Al Capone purchased a sprawling estate on Miami Beach’s Palm Island, seeking.
articles.body: In 1928, at the height of his reign as Chicago’s most notorious gangster, Al Capone purchased a sprawling estate on Miami Beach’s Palm Island, seeking a warm-weather retreat from the cold and his foes. He is reported to have spent some $200,000 bolstering the property with bulletproof walls, steel shutters and other security measures befitting a man who lived under threat of attack at every turn. Nearly a century later, the mansion that once was home to “Scarface” is no more, demolished in 2023 after years of deterioration and fruitless attempts at preservation. Now, the vacant waterfront lot where the infamous home once stood has sold for $21 million, a stark reminder of how land values in Miami Beach have outpaced even the most notorious chapters of local history, according to a report by Profile Miami Real Estate.Capone’s Miami escapeAl Capone first visited Miami in the mid-1920s, drawn by the warm climate, booming real estate market and the city’s reputation as a playground for the wealthy and the criminal. In 1928, he bought a large estate on Palm Island, a man-made, exclusive enclave in Biscayne Bay that was already attracting millionaires, celebrities and politicians. The house itself was a substantial Mediterranean Revival mansion, with multiple bedrooms, grand entertaining spaces and sweeping views of the bay. But Capone was not just looking for luxury. According to local histories and real estate accounts, he invested heavily in security, installing reinforced concrete walls, steel shutters and other fortifications designed to withstand an attack. For a man who had survived numerous assassination attempts and was constantly pursued by law enforcement and rival gangs, the Miami estate was meant to be a fortress as much as a home.From gangster hideout to local landmarkCapone used the Palm Island house as a winter retreat throughout the late 1920s and early 1930s, hosting parties and conducting business while ostensibly “on vacation.” He was eventually convicted of tax evasion in 1931 and sent to prison, after which his grip on the property loosened. The house changed hands several times over the decades, serving at various points as a private residence, a boarding house and, in some accounts, a short-term rental property. As Miami Beach evolved from a sleepy resort town to a global real estate hot spot, the Capone estate became a curious footnote: a piece of criminal history sitting on increasingly valuable land. By the end of the 20th century the mansion was in desperate need of repair with water damage, structural issues and years of neglect taking their toll.Years of decay and failed preservationDespite its notorious provenance, the Capone house never received formal historic designation that would have protected it from demolition. Over the years, various owners and developers floated plans to restore or repurpose the structure but none came to fruition. The cost of bringing the rundown mansion up to modern codes, combined with the enormous underlying land value made preservation a financial non-starter. By the 2010s the property was commonly referred to as a “teardown” in real estate circles, with the house seen as more a hindrance than a help.Reactions from neighbors and local historians were split. Some lamented the disappearance of a physical link to Miami’s vibrant history, while others considered the dilapidated building an eyesore on an otherwise immaculate island. Demolition in 2023 Following years of legal and logistical hurdles, the Capone mansion was ultimately razed in 2023. Workers knocked down the decaying walls, carted away rubble and vacated the site, transforming it into a vacant, waterfront lot where the mobster once roamed. The demolition marked the end of nearly a century of physical presence for one of Miami Beach’s most infamous addresses.With the house gone, the site’s value was now purely about location: a large, buildable lot on Palm Island with direct bay frontage, privacy and proximity to Miami Beach’s amenities. In today’s market, that combination is extraordinarily rare—and extraordinarily expensive.A $21 million vacant lotIn August 2026, the former Capone estate site sold for $21 million, according to local real estate reporting. The buyer is reported to be a private purchaser or entity planning to build a new, ultra-luxury home on the parcel, though specific details were not immediately disclosed.At $21 million, the sale price reflects several realities of the current Miami Beach market. This includes: severe scarcity of large, waterfront lots on exclusive islands like Palm Island; strong demand from domestic and international buyers seeking privacy, security and prestige; and a broader trend in which land values in top neighbourhoods have far outpaced the value of older structures sitting on them.For context, Capone originally bought the estate in 1928 for a fraction of that amount, even adjusted for inflation. The $200,000 he reportedly spent on fortifications would also be a small fraction of today’s sale price, underscoring how dramatically the economics of Miami Beach real estate have shifted over nearly a century.What might rise in Capone’s placeWhile no official plans have been announced, the most likely outcome for the site is a brand-new, custom-built mansion designed for a high-net-worth buyer. Palm Island is known for its large, contemporary estates, many with private docks, pools and extensive security systems—amenities that would appeal to the same kind of buyer who might appreciate the Capone name, even if the original house is gone. Some local observers have speculated that a developer could choose to reference the property’s history in subtle ways, through naming, design motifs or marketing, though any new structure will inevitably reflect 21st-century tastes and technology rather than 1920s glamour.A symbol of Miami’s changing landscapeThe sale of the former Capone estate site for $21 million is more than a real estate transaction; it’s a symbol of how Miami Beach has transformed since the gangster era. What was once a hideout for a notorious criminal is now a ultra-high-value parcel in one of the most exclusive neighbourhoods in South Florida. For historians and preservationists, the demolition and sale highlight the challenges of saving older buildings in a market where land is often worth far more than the structures on it. For developers and buyers, the site represents a rare opportunity to build a legacy home on a plot with a story that no amount of new construction can fully replicate.The legacy that remainsThough the mansion is gone, the story of Al Capone’s Miami estate endures in local lore, tour guides and real estate anecdotes. The image of a bulletproof gangster fortress on a tranquil island continues to capture the imagination, even as the physical evidence disappears.In the end, the $21 million sale price is less about Capone and more about Miami Beach itself: a place where history, hype and hard numbers collide, and where even a vacant lot can carry the weight of a legend.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: In 1993, Barbra Streisand gave her $15 million Malibu estate to conservation; the 24-acre property was planned as an environmental research centre
articles.summary: US News: For years, Barbra Streisand’s Ramirez Canyon estate had been a private Malibu retreat, complete with five houses, landscaped grounds and interiors ref.
articles.body: For years, Barbra Streisand’s Ramirez Canyon estate had been a private Malibu retreat, complete with five houses, landscaped grounds and interiors reflecting her fascination with Art Deco.The property had proved difficult to sell, remaining on the market from 1987 until 1993, while its listing price fell from $18 million to $11.5 million. Then Streisand chose a very different future for the estate. According to Los Angeles Times, in November 1993, she agreed to donate the roughly 17,000-square-foot property to the Santa Monica Mountains Conservancy, with state appraisers valuing the gift at $15 million. The plan went beyond simply protecting the land.The conservancy envisioned an environmental research centre, space for visiting scholars and researchers, conferences and eventual public access. For Streisand, the donation offered a way to keep the unusual estate together rather than see it gradually divided or lose the character that had made it distinctive.Barbra Streisand’s Ramirez Canyon property became a $15 million conservation giftThe Ramirez Canyon property was not an ordinary piece of undeveloped mountain land. Five houses stood across the estate, arranged among trees and gardens, with the buildings collectively covering roughly 17,000 square feet.For years, the property had also been on the real estate market. It was listed in 1987 and remained available until the summer of 1993. Its asking price had reportedly begun at $18 million before eventually falling to $11.5 million.By then, Streisand had started discussing another possibility with the Santa Monica Mountains Conservancy. The conversations began around three months before the donation was announced.State appraisers valued the estate at $15 million, making it, according to the conservancy's executive director Joseph T. Edmiston, the most valuable property ever donated to the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area at that point, as reported by Los Angeles Times.New conservation centre was planned for the heart of the Malibu estateThe plan was not simply to preserve the estate as an untouched piece of Malibu. The conservancy intended to establish an environmental research complex there, called the Streisand Center for Conservancy Studies.The buildings were expected to provide space for environmental work, including a scholars-in-residence programme. Edmiston said the centre could accommodate visiting academics and researchers studying land conservation and related subjects.Part of the grounds was also expected to be opened to the public. The location offered a possible connection with the existing trail network through the Santa Monica Mountains, giving the property a role beyond research and administration.The conservancy was due to take possession on December 1, 1993. Its first planned conference was scheduled for February and was to focus on greenways including former rights of way, railway routes and other corridors that could be incorporated into urban park systems.The property’s history stretched from political concerts to Art Deco interiorsThe estate had already played a public role before its donation. In 1986, Streisand hosted a benefit concert there for Democratic senatorial candidates. The event was taped for cable television and marked her first public performance in six years.Reportedly, the concert raised $1.5 million for the political candidates. The televised programme also generated an estimated $7 million for charities and causes supported by Streisand.Away from the concert, the property was known for its collection of distinctive houses and its carefully designed interiors. One of the residences was featured in Architectural Digest in late 1993, with particular attention given to Streisand's interest in Art Deco design.That house contained an extensive collection of period furniture and decorative objects. Much of the collection was due to be offered at auction in New York the following March.The plan aimed to preserve the estate’s distinctive architecture and interiorsThe estate's buildings were not expected to disappear simply because the land was moving into conservation ownership. Edmiston described the collection of structures as part of what made the property suitable for the proposed centre.There was an English country-estate quality to the grounds, alongside several different architectural styles. Two of the houses had a country character, with one resembling a heavily remodelled barn. Another was a Mediterranean-style villa with a projection room measuring about 2,000 square feet.The conservancy was also interested in retaining some of the furnishings. Rather than stripping the buildings of their interiors, officials hoped Streisand might donate at least part of the Art Deco collection as well. If that was not possible, they considered purchasing selected pieces.A major addition to the Santa Monica MountainsEdmiston said, “There have been three major donations in the history of the Santa Monica Mountains”.The Santa Monica Mountains Conservancy had been established in 1981, with responsibilities that included acquiring land in the mountains and supporting environmental education. By the time of Streisand's gift, it had acquired about 20,000 acres.The organisation placed the new donation alongside two earlier major private gifts. The first was the 186-acre Will Rogers estate, which entered the state park system in 1944. At the time, that property had been valued at $550,000.The other was the 10-acre oceanfront estate of actor Leo Carrillo, donated later and valued at $300,000.Streisand's property was considerably larger in both its appraised value and the scale of its buildings. Its intended use also reflected the conservancy's expanding interest in research and environmental education.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Charlie Kirk murder case goes to trial; accused Tyler Robinson pleads 'not guilty' on all charges
articles.summary: US News: Tyler Robinson, the Utah man accused of killing conservative activist Charlie Kirk, has pleaded not guilty to all charges, including aggravated murder.
articles.body: Tyler Robinson, the Utah man accused of killing conservative activist Charlie Kirk, has pleaded not guilty to all charges, including aggravated murder, after a judge ruled that the case can proceed to trial. Robinson could face the death penalty if convicted.Utah District Judge Tony Graf on Tuesday ruled that prosecutors had presented enough evidence to pursue the aggravated murder charge, siding with prosecutors who said they had a “mountain of evidence” against Robinson, 23.Prosecutors allege Robinson fatally shot Kirk while he was speaking to a crowd of more than 3,000 people at Utah Valley University in September 2025. Robinson turned himself in a day after the shooting.According to prosecutors, Robinson fired a high-powered, bolt-action rifle from a rooftop more than 400 feet (122 metres) away. They argue that he knew he could miss Kirk and strike someone else in the crowd. Prosecutor Ryan McBride said Robinson shot Kirk because he disagreed with his political views.The defence had sought to block the aggravated murder charge from going to trial or remove the possibility of the death penalty. Defence attorney Staci Visser argued that prosecutors had failed to establish the level of risk to others required under Utah law.“There was one shot. One bullet. One victim,” Visser argued, saying Kirk was elevated on a stage and was not immediately near others when he was shot in the neck.Prosecutor Chad Grunander countered that Robinson was armed with a bolt-action rifle loaded with additional rounds, arguing that he “came prepared to shoot again.”Graf nevertheless ruled that the aggravated murder charge could proceed, citing, among other factors, the positions of people in and around the tent where Kirk was speaking. A lesser murder charge would carry a minimum sentence of 15 years and a maximum of life in prison.During a five-day hearing in July, prosecutors presented DNA evidence they said linked Robinson to the rifle and to a tool allegedly used to engrave ammunition. Defence lawyers questioned the reliability of the DNA evidence.Prosecutors also presented a handwritten note they said Robinson left for his romantic partner before the shooting. The note allegedly said: “I had the opportunity to take out Charlie Kirk, and I took it.”Prosecutors are also seeking sentencing enhancements by alleging that Kirk was targeted because of his political beliefs. They cited an inscription on a bullet found in the rifle as evidence of a political motive, as well as a text message allegedly written by Robinson that said: “I had enough of his hatred. Some hate can’t be negotiated out.”The defence has disputed the evidence of a political motive.Kirk’s family welcomed the judge’s decision, calling it “an important step” in their pursuit of justice. His parents, Robert and Kathryn Kirk, attended the hearing at the heavily secured courthouse in Provo alongside his widow, Erika Kirk.A few dozen local members of Turning Point USA, the conservative youth organisation Kirk helped build, gathered outside the courthouse.Robinson showed little visible reaction during the hearing, while his mother cried.The case will now move towards trial, where prosecutors will have to prove the aggravated murder charge and the alleged political motive beyond a reasonable doubt.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: US News: The former Tropical Storm Edouard deteriorated into a depression on Tuesday while delivering powerful gusts and heavy rains on portions of Texas, caus.
articles.body: The former Tropical Storm Edouard deteriorated into a depression on Tuesday while delivering powerful gusts and heavy rains on portions of Texas, causing thousands of people to lose power, falling trees, and flooding highways.According to the National Hurricane Center, the storm reached Johnson Bayou, Louisiana, a tiny coastal town, with maximum sustained winds of 60 mph (95 kph). Forecasters predicted that it will continue to weaken until disappearing this week as it proceeded inland and passed across southeastern Texas.Meanwhile, a number of storms, including Lowell, which earlier in the day attained hurricane intensity, were building in the Pacific Ocean.Edouard was predicted to produce 3 to 7 inches (8 to 17 centimeters) of rain, with a maximum of 12 inches (30 centimeters), according to the hurricane center. Less was expected in southwestern Louisiana.Brad Reinhart, a senior hurricane expert at the National Hurricane Center stated, "that rainfall could produce some flash flooding and river flooding."A storm hits the Texas-Louisiana borderThe Texas Office of Emergency Management advised citizens to avoid the road when the storm's core moved over Beaumont, Texas, which is located approximately 80 miles (130 kilometers) northeast of Houston. The city's offices were closed.Beaumont Police said on social media that there were felled trees obstructing roadways, broken traffic lights, and flooded underpasses all around the city.According to the poweroutage.com report, around 32,000 utility customers in Jefferson county, which includes Beaumont, were without electricity.Mike Gilbert made the decision to close his surf store in Crystal Beach, Texas, ahead of the hurricane because he didn't want to put his staff at danger of having trouble returning home. However, he claimed that when Edouard made landfall around 60 miles (96 kilometers) northeast of his place on Tuesday, all that was left were gloomy sky and light rain.Gilbert said, "You literally never know." "It could have been a completely different story if it had suddenly moved over 50 miles and picked up 20 mph in the wind."Connor Salvador, the owner of an RV park along the ocean in Cameron, Louisiana, reported that by Tuesday morning, the gusts had increased and intermittent rain was falling. He stated that he wasn't too concerned about Edouard, even if there may be a "little bit" of flooding in case they receive a lot of rain.He remarked, "We're pretty used to all these types of storms that come through."Numerous storms in the PacificAccording to forecasters, newly formed storm Lowell in the Pacific ocean is predicted to stay several hundred miles from Hawaii for the next several days at least. However, swells from the storm are expected to affect portions of the islands starting on Wednesday."This hurricane is likely to increase the surf and make for dangerous beach conditions and marine conditions for any boaters near the Hawaiian islands over the next few days", said by National Hurricane Center forecaster Andrew Hagan.Tropical Storm Marie developed in the Pacific Ocean early on Tuesday, well offshore of southwest Mexico as per the center.It was predicted by forecasters to develop into a hurricane by Wednesday night, and over the next several days, swells from the storm were also expected to impact portions of the coast in southwest Mexico and the Baja California peninsula.Driven by warm waters far from any land, Karina developed into a hurricane on Sunday in other parts of the Pacific. Forecasters stated on Tuesday that it was predicted to diminish after it intensified into a strong category 4 storm on Monday.The hurricane center reported that portions of Haiti, the Dominican Republic, the Turks and Caicos, and the Bahamas saw rain and thunderstorms due to the remnants of Tropical Storm Dolly.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In the 1980s, Michael Jackson put his 2,700-acre California ranch under an agricultural preservation programme; years later, officials found an amusement park, a zoo and other unapproved developments
articles.summary: US News: Michael Jackson's sprawling Neverland Ranch in California benefited for years from a state agricultural land-preservation programme that reduced its p.
articles.body: Michael Jackson's sprawling Neverland Ranch in California benefited for years from a state agricultural land-preservation programme that reduced its property-tax burden, but the arrangement came under scrutiny after county officials discovered extensive development on parts of the estate. The roughly 2,700-acre ranch in Santa Barbara County included Jackson's home, an amusement park, zoo and other entertainment facilities, while much of the property was also used for cattle grazing. In 2003, county officials said Jackson had failed to obtain required permits or comply with zoning rules for a number of developments built over the previous decade. The dispute eventually led to about 70 acres being removed from the agricultural preservation programme, potentially increasing Jackson's annual property taxes by tens of thousands of dollars.Michael Jackson's 2,700-acre ranch had a tax-saving secretThe secret behind the lower tax bill was California's Williamson Act, a land-preservation programme created to encourage owners to keep agricultural land in farming and compatible open-space uses. Rather than taxing qualifying property according to its full potential development value, the programme allowed land under contract to receive a lower assessment based on its restricted use and agricultural income potential. Neverland qualified in part because Jackson legitimately leased most of the ranch to a cattle-ranching operation. The arrangement meant that the enormous property, despite being known worldwide for its lavish entertainment facilities, also had a genuine agricultural use that allowed qualifying portions to receive preferential property-tax treatment.How the Williamson Act workedCalifornia introduced the Williamson Act in 1965 to discourage the premature conversion of agricultural land to urban and other higher-value uses. Landowners who entered contracts agreed to keep their property in agricultural or compatible open-space uses for a specified period, while receiving reduced property-tax assessments in return. The programme was intended to make it financially attractive for owners to preserve farmland rather than sell or develop it.The arrangement was not a special tax break created for Jackson. It was a statewide programme available to qualifying agricultural properties. The unusual element at Neverland was the combination of agricultural land with a vast private entertainment estate containing attractions that were far removed from conventional ranching.Neverland was more than a cattle ranchJackson purchased the property in the 1980s and transformed it into Neverland Ranch, creating a private world that included his residence, amusement-park attractions, a zoo and other recreational facilities. Yet most of the ranch remained connected to agricultural use, with cattle grazing carried out through a ranching operation.That combination eventually became important to county officials. The agricultural-preservation programme did not simply mean that every square metre of Neverland had to remain completely untouched. Rather, land covered by the agreement was subject to restrictions governing agricultural and compatible uses. The county therefore had to determine whether the developed portions of the estate complied with the applicable rules.County officials began questioning the developmentThe issue came to a head in 2003, when Santa Barbara County officials investigated development at Neverland. County planners had raised concerns about the sprawling amusement-park area, prompting the county Agricultural Commissioner to request a report from the planning department.Officials said they discovered that Jackson had failed to obtain building permits or comply with zoning ordinances for a range of developments carried out over approximately 10 years. The investigation raised questions not only about the individual structures but also about whether the extent of development was compatible with the property's agricultural-preserve status.An amusement park and zoo became part of the disputeThe developments identified by county officials included some relatively ordinary structures as well as highly unusual features. They said permits should have been obtained for a gatehouse, a three-car garage, a primate centre, a go-kart track, seven amusement-park rides and a giant outdoor movie screen.Neverland's amusement park and zoo were particularly significant because they illustrated how extensively parts of the ranch had been transformed for recreational use. County officials said Jackson had followed permit procedures and zoning rules for some of his developed property, but not for all of the rides and other construction.About 70 acres were removed from the programmeIn September 2003, the Santa Barbara County Board of Supervisors voted 4-0 to accept Jackson's proposal to remove his house, amusement park, zoo and several other buildings from the agricultural-preserve programme. County officials said about 70 acres were involved.The decision did not mean that the entire 2,700-acre property suddenly ceased to have an agricultural connection. Instead, the affected developed portions were removed from the programme, separating those areas from the land that could continue to qualify under the agricultural-preservation arrangement.Jackson could lose tens of thousands in annual tax savingsThe change had a direct financial consequence. Santa Barbara County officials estimated that Jackson had been saving about $70,000 a year in property taxes through the agricultural-preserve arrangement.The county assessor's office placed the 2002-03 assessed value of Neverland at $12,292,618. Jackson's property taxes that year were estimated at about $130,000. County officials said that without the tax benefit, the property's overall assessed value could rise by about $6 million, potentially increasing annual property taxes to around $200,000.Those figures were contemporary county estimates, so they are best presented as estimates rather than as a definitive calculation of Jackson's long-term tax liability.The tax increase was phased inJackson did not simply go from paying the lower tax amount to the full estimated amount overnight. Under the Williamson Act system, land leaving an agricultural-preserve contract can enter a nine-year non-renewal period during which its assessment gradually moves towards the level that would apply without the restrictions.Santa Barbara County officials said Jackson's tax payments would therefore increase over a nine-year period beginning in January. The gradual process reflected the way California's agricultural-preservation system handled the removal of land from its tax-benefit arrangement.The permit problems were separate from the tax issueThe Neverland controversy involved two connected but distinct issues. One was whether the developed portions of the property could continue receiving the agricultural tax treatment. The other concerned whether Jackson had obtained the necessary permits and complied with county zoning requirements.Officials were considering possible legal action over back taxes and potential fines related to the permit and zoning violations. However, the contemporary reports do not establish that Jackson was convicted of tax fraud or deliberately engaged in tax evasion. Describing the episode as a tax-fraud case would therefore go beyond the evidence.Why the ranch's agricultural use matteredThe fact that most of Neverland was associated with cattle grazing was central to the story. County officials said Jackson legitimately leased most of the property to a cattle-ranching operation, giving the ranch a genuine agricultural use.That agricultural activity allowed the property to benefit from a programme intended to protect working agricultural land. The controversy arose when county officials examined how that agricultural use coexisted with the extensive amusement and recreational development on the estate.In other words, the unusual feature was not simply that a celebrity received an agricultural tax benefit. It was that one of California's most famous private estates combined a working ranch with an amusement park, zoo and other highly developed facilities.Neverland exposed the wider appeal of ranch tax breaksThe case also highlighted why large ranches can be financially attractive to wealthy landowners. California's agricultural-preservation system can reduce property taxes when landowners agree to restrictions designed to preserve agricultural use.For owners of very large properties, even a relatively modest difference in the tax assessment can translate into substantial annual savings. The system therefore creates a financial incentive to maintain agricultural land rather than convert it to more intensive development.The Neverland case showed the other side of that bargain. The tax advantage came with conditions, and development that did not comply with those conditions could result in land being removed from the programme and the tax benefit being reduced.Neverland later became part of Jackson's financial troublesThe tax dispute emerged at a time when Jackson was facing growing financial difficulties. His problems eventually extended to the ownership of Neverland itself.In 2008, the ranch became subject to foreclosure proceedings after a loan connected to the property went into default. An investment company associated with Colony Capital acquired the loan, and the property was subsequently placed into a joint venture.Jackson died in 2009, and the property was later renamed Sycamore Valley Ranch. In 2020, billionaire Ron Burkle purchased the estate for a reported $22 million.The tax-saving secret behind NeverlandThe Neverland story was not about Jackson receiving a special celebrity-only tax deal. His property benefited from a California programme that was designed to encourage agricultural landowners to preserve their land for farming and compatible uses. The ranch's cattle operation helped it qualify, while the extraordinary development of parts of the estate eventually brought the arrangement under scrutiny.When Santa Barbara County officials found unpermitted or non-compliant development, including amusement-park attractions and a zoo, about 70 acres were removed from the agricultural-preserve programme. Jackson was then facing the loss of a tax benefit estimated at roughly $70,000 a year, with the increase in his property taxes phased in over time.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Four California seniors reported scams in just 24 hours; police say cryptocurrency, gift-card and timeshare schemes cost them more than $315,000
articles.summary: US News: Four seniors in Petaluma, California, have reported separate scams within just 24 hours, with suspected losses adding up to more than $315,000.The cas.
articles.body: Four seniors in Petaluma, California, have reported separate scams within just 24 hours, with suspected losses adding up to more than $315,000.The cases involved cryptocurrency, timeshares and gift cards. Petaluma police said officers responded to four separate reports from seniors who had been targeted through these schemes during the same period, Patch reported.The incidents have prompted police to warn residents to be careful when anyone asks them to send money. Officers said people should take time to check who is asking for the payment and whether the request is genuine before handing over money.The warning is particularly important for Petaluma, where people aged 65 and above make up more than 22% of the population, according to police. The department said this makes the community especially likely to see scams aimed at older residents.4 scams, 24 hoursThe four reports involved different types of scams, but they had one common element. Seniors were persuaded to give money through methods that were fraudulent.In one type of scheme, scammers used cryptocurrency. Cryptocurrency payments can be difficult to recover once they have been sent, making such demands particularly concerning for people who may not be familiar with digital currencies.Another reported scheme involved timeshares. Timeshare-related scams can involve requests for money connected to a property or an alleged transaction.Gift cards were also involved in one of the reported scams. Gift cards are sometimes used by scammers because they can ask victims to purchase cards and then share the card details or codes.Police said the suspected losses from all four incidents totalled more than $315,000. The department did not provide individual amounts for each case in its warning.The reports came within a short period, prompting Petaluma police to remind residents that scammers may try to create a sense of urgency.Police warn of pressure tacticsAccording to Petaluma police, scammers often tell people that their financial demands require immediate action. This pressure can make victims feel that they have to send money before they have time to check the request. Police warned that legitimate organisations will not pressure people to pay on the spot.Residents were advised to stop and check the request instead of acting immediately. Police said people should research the person or company involved and contact companies directly to confirm whether a payment request is genuine.The department also encouraged residents to speak to family members when they are unsure about a financial request. Asking another person for advice can give someone time to check whether the situation is legitimate before making a payment.Helping seniors stay safePetaluma police said the department shares scam-prevention information online and also holds presentations in person. However, officers said residents also have a role to play in protecting older members of the community.The department urged people to check in with elderly neighbours and loved ones. Regular conversations can help families and neighbours identify suspicious requests and ensure that older residents do not become the next victims of a scam.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A Florida family listed its 42.57-acre Clearwater Beach estate for $37.5 million; the state now wants about 28 undeveloped acres to expand Caladesi Island State Park
articles.summary: US News: On one of the last large, undeveloped stretches of land near Clearwater Beach, a 42.57-acre family estate has sat on the market for $37.5 million, dra.
articles.body: On one of the last large, undeveloped stretches of land near Clearwater Beach, a 42.57-acre family estate has sat on the market for $37.5 million, drawing attention from luxury buyers and conservationists alike. Now, the state of Florida has entered the picture, expressing interest in acquiring roughly 28 acres of the property to expand Caladesi Island State Park and protect critical coastal habitat. As reported by AOL and in preliminary evaluations by the Florida Natural Areas Inventory, the potential deal would preserve mangroves, tidal creeks and wildlife corridors while limiting future development on a key parcel along the Intracoastal Waterway. Read on to know more here:A rare large holding near Clearwater BeachThe estate, owned by a local family for decades, occupies a sprawling 42.57-acre site on the Clearwater Beach side of the Intracoastal, just south of the causeway that connects the barrier island to the mainland. In a region where most parcels have long been subdivided into condos, hotels and single-family homes, a holding of this size is exceptionally rare.The property includes a mix of developed and undeveloped land: a private residence, docks and outbuildings on a portion of the site, with the majority remaining as natural coastal habitat—mangrove forests, tidal wetlands, pine flatwoods and open meadows. That combination of location and natural character is what makes it both valuable to developers and attractive to conservationists.The $37.5 million listingThe family listed the estate for $37.5 million, positioning it as a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity for a buyer seeking privacy, water access and a large land bank in one of Florida’s most desirable coastal markets. At that price, the property is among the most expensive residential listings in the Clearwater area, reflecting not just the land’s size but also its waterfront position and development potential.For years, the owners have resisted pressure to sell or subdivide, preferring to keep the land intact. But as the family’s circumstances changed and the property’s maintenance costs grew, they decided to test the market, knowing that any sale would likely reshape this corner of Clearwater Beach.The state’s conservation interestAlmost as soon as the listing became widely known, state officials and conservation groups began looking at the property through a different lens. Caladesi Island State Park, which lies just across the Intracoastal from the estate, is one of the few remaining largely undeveloped barrier islands in the Tampa Bay region. The park protects beaches, dunes, mangroves and important nesting habitat for shorebirds and sea turtles.According to preliminary evaluations by the Florida Natural Areas Inventory (FNAI), the undeveloped portion of the Clearwater Beach estate, roughly 28 acres, contains high-quality natural communities that would significantly enhance the park if added to its boundaries. These include: mangrove forests and tidal creeks that serve as nurseries for fish and shellfish; coastal hammocks and pine flatwoods that provide habitat for native birds and small mammals; and buffer zones that help protect the park and neighbouring properties from storm surge and erosion.State agencies, including the Florida Department of Environmental Protection and Florida Forest Service, have begun exploring whether Florida Forever or other conservation funding programs could be used to acquire the land.Why this parcel matters for Caladesi Island State ParkCaladesi Island State Park is already a critical piece of the region’s conservation network, but it is surrounded by development on multiple sides. Adding the 28 acres from the Clearwater Beach estate would: expand the park’s footprint along the Intracoastal, creating a larger contiguous protected area; strengthen wildlife corridors that allow animals to move between habitats without crossing busy roads or developed zones; improve water quality by preserving mangroves and wetlands that filter runoff before it reaches the bay; and provide additional buffer against sea-level rise and stronger storms, which are increasingly threatening low-lying coastal parks.For conservation planners, the opportunity to add such a large, ecologically valuable parcel so close to an existing park is rare, especially in a heavily developed county like Pinellas.The family’s position and community reactionThe owning family has not publicly committed to selling to the state, but representatives have indicated they are open to discussions that respect both their financial interests and the land’s conservation value. Any deal would need to balance the $37.5 million listing price against what the state can realistically pay using available conservation funds, which are often limited and competitive.Local reaction has been mixed. Some residents and business owners worry that a state acquisition could limit future economic development or reduce the tax base. Others, including environmental groups and many neighbours, see the potential park expansion as a once-in-a-generation chance to lock in open space and protect wildlife in an area that has seen intense development pressure.Funding and the path forwardIf the state moves forward, the purchase would likely be structured through Florida Forever, the state’s landmark conservation program that uses bond funding to acquire high-priority lands for parks, greenways and wildlife corridors. The FNAI preliminary evaluation, which rates properties based on their ecological significance and urgency, is often a key step in determining which lands qualify for such funding.Even if the state cannot acquire the entire 28-acre conservation target immediately, there are other possible arrangements, such as: purchasing the land in phases as funding becomes available; using conservation easements to protect the habitat while allowing limited private use on certain portions; and partnering with nonprofit land trusts to bridge funding gaps and manage the property.What’s at stakeAt its core, this situation is about more than one family’s estate or one park’s boundary. It’s about how Florida chooses to manage its remaining coastal wildlands in the face of rising property values, population growth and climate change.If the state succeeds in acquiring the 28 acres, Caladesi Island State Park will gain a significant expansion that could protect critical habitat for decades to come. If the land is sold for private development instead, the area will likely see new homes, docks and landscaping that fragment the habitat and reduce the ecological connectivity that conservationists value.For now, the 42.57-acre Clearwater Beach estate remains on the market, a large, green swath on maps that are otherwise crowded with rooftops and roads. Whether it becomes part of a state park or a new luxury enclave will depend on negotiations, funding and the choices made by a family that has guarded this land for generations.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Nepal flood death toll rises to 1,127
articles.summary: The death toll in Nepal from last week's devastating flooding in the Himalayas has risen to 1,127, police said on Wednesday. Of the bodies recovered so far,...
articles.body:
Nepal's death toll from recent flooding reaches 1,127, with identification efforts ongoing for recovered bodies.

Only 95 bodies out of those recovered have been returned to families, as the full scale of the disaster remains unclear.

World Health Organization warns of disease outbreaks in affected areas due to large numbers of displaced people living in unsanitary conditions.

The death toll in Nepal from last week's devastating flooding in the Himalayas has risen to 1,127, police said on Wednesday.

Of the bodies recovered so far, only 95 had been handed over to affected families by Wednesday morning, according to Nepalese police. China's death toll for the Tibet region has stood at 16 for several days.

One week on, the full scale of the disaster remains unclear.

The catastrophic flash flood, carrying water, mud, ice and debris, swept away everything in its path in the border region. Experts believe a massive glacier collapse on the Tibetan side triggered the disaster.

The death toll in Nepal alone passed 1,000 on Tuesday, while more than 4,600 people were reported missing.

Most of the bodies recovered so far have not been identified. Authorities said rescuers were often finding only bone fragments or other human remains.

All recovered remains could, however, be identified through DNA analysis, according to authorities.

The World Health Organization has warned of the risk of disease outbreaks in the affected areas.

Large numbers of displaced people living in cramped conditions, together with flooding and stagnant water, increased the risk of infectious diseases spreading, the WHO said.
